questions.q: Which set correctly lists all four Bell states?
questions.explain: The four Bell states pair up the computational basis states with plus and minus relative phases: (|00⟩±|11⟩)/√2 and (|01⟩±|10⟩)/√2. The other options list the plain computational basis, single-qubit states, or product states — none of which are the maximally entangled Bell basis.

questions.q: Starting from |00⟩, applying a Hadamard to qubit 1 produces (|00⟩+|10⟩)/√2. What does applying CNOT (qubit 1 as control, qubit 2 as target) to that state produce?
options: (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, because the |00⟩ term is unchanged (control is 0) while the |10⟩ term has its target flipped to give |11⟩ (control is 1)
(|10⟩+|01⟩)/√2, because CNOT swaps the two qubits
questions.explain: CNOT flips the target only when the control is |1⟩. Applied term by term: the |00⟩ term has control 0, so it's untouched; the |10⟩ term has control 1, so its target flips from 0 to 1, becoming |11⟩. The result is (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 = |Φ+⟩.

questions.q: If you measure qubit 1 of |Φ+⟩ and get the outcome 0, what can you say about qubit 2 with certainty?
options: Nothing — qubit 2's outcome is still a 50/50 coin flip
Qubit 2 has already been destroyed by the measurement
questions.explain: For |Φ+⟩, P(00)=P(11)=0.5 exactly, and P(01)=P(10)=0 exactly. So once qubit 1 measures 0, the only consistent outcome for qubit 2 is also 0 — a certainty, not a probability.

questions.q: Before either qubit of |Φ+⟩ is measured, what is the probability that qubit 1 alone measures 0?
options: 1.0 — qubit 1 is already determined to be 0
0.5 — qubit 1's own marginal outcome is a perfect coin flip, just like a single |+⟩ qubit
It is undefined because qubit 1 has no individual state
questions.explain: Qubit 1's marginal probability is exactly 0.5 for each outcome — nothing unusual on its own. What's remarkable is not qubit 1's individual statistics, but its perfect correlation with qubit 2 once both are compared.

questions.q: Why are the Bell states specifically called "maximally entangled"?
options: Because they take the longest circuit to prepare
Because they use the most qubits of any entangled state
Because, for a two-qubit system, no state produces stronger per-measurement correlation between its two qubits than a Bell state does
Because they can only be created using Hadamard gates
questions.explain: "Maximally entangled" is a precise claim: among all possible two-qubit states, the Bell states sit at the extreme of achievable correlation strength, which is exactly why they're the standard building block for teleportation and superdense coding.
